lines: Every engine you met this chapter earned its place by being read straight from its own source, never assumed.
That discipline alone doesn't answer the one question an engineer actually has to decide.
This closing topic puts six engines side by side and asks exactly that question.
You could stop here and just set six vendors' claims against each other.
But one of these six engines is sitting right here, with a real table this chapter already built.
answer: Running it for real settles one number outright, no vendor claim needed.
Everything this sandbox can't run still gets a sourced number standing next to it.

lines: Three of these six you already ran with your own hands earlier in this chapter.
The other three you only ever read about, and that was by design, not a shortcut.
Lining all six up together is the entire point of today.
Notice neither side solves concurrency by making one query run faster.
Both sides solve it by giving more queries somewhere else to run at the same time.
The difference is only who owns the machines doing that running.
A query optimizer choosing a join order is not the same thing as a service rewriting your table overnight.
One reacts to a single query passing through; the other reshapes the data every later query will hit.
Only the warehouses you met this chapter do that second, deeper kind of tuning.
This is the one moment this topic can actually run something, instead of only reading about it.
A real scan against a real table on this very machine is about to happen.
answer: A smaller priced unit still wins out once you convert it to match the other vendor's unit.
The published rate that looks cheaper on paper isn't the one that prices this scan lower.

lines: That number a moment ago wasn't narrated for you, it came straight out of a real query plan.
Everything downstream of it stays a real number, just handed two different published multipliers to wear.
That gap between measuring and estimating is the one thing this topic refuses to blur.
An engine with no catalog of its own can't lock you in, because it owns nothing of yours to keep.
A warehouse's governance lives inside the very account that also bills you for crossing a region boundary.
Neither choice is free, they simply charge you in a different currency.
None of this says the open side always wins, or that the managed side always wins either.
It says pay close attention to what you are actually buying when you pick one of them.
Pooled concurrency and governance that comes built in are real purchases, not just marketing language.
Every engine in this chapter turned stored data into an answer, each on the terms its own documentation set.
Nothing it built along the way turned that stored data into more stored data at real scale.
That is exactly where the next chapter begins.
